question: to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE) Subject:

A 2024 study conducted by Yield Sec on behalf of the European Casino Association found that 71 % of online gambling activity targeting European users takes place on unlicensed, and thus illegal, websites. At the same time, the overall use of online gambling in the EU has continued to increase. Recent reports further indicate that illegal gambling websites are frequently promoted by content creators, particularly on video platforms such as YouTube and Twitch. Such promotion is often carried out through affiliate links, enabling content creators to receive a percentage or fixed payment for each new player they bring on board. The users reached through such promotional activities are often young and potentially vulnerable. Content that promotes unlicensed online gambling services is illegal and should therefore be removed by online platforms in accordance with the Digital Services Act1. Nevertheless, a significant amount of such promotional content appears to remain available online. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the active promotion, by online content creators in the EU, of unlicensed online gambling services?
Does the Commission intend to investigate the issue further?
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure the more effective enforcement of the Digital Services Act?

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the issue of undisclosed advertising on online platforms, as well as the promotion of illegal products online. The Digital Services Act1 (DSA) requires online platforms to provide a user-friendly notice and action mechanism ensuring users can report content, including advertisements, they consider to be illegal. Additionally, very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are required to diligently assess and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including risks concerning the dissemination of illegal content The guidelines on the protection of minors2 under the DSA clarify that minors should not be exposed to advertising for products that could negatively impact their privacy, safety and security, and any commercial content should be clearly labelled as such. The protection of minors as consumers is also a priority under the upcoming Digital Fairness Act, which will address issues such as unfair influencer marketing. The Commission is closely monitoring VLOPs and VLOSEs with the DSA. For example, the Commission has adopted preliminary findings against the provider of Facebook and Instagram for appearing to have failed to provide users with a user-friendly and easily accessible notice and action mechanism. The Commission also recently opened formal proceedings against the provider of Snapchat due to suspicions relating to, among other issues, the failure to address risks linked to the promotion of prohibited or age-restricted products to minors. Lastly, the Commission is looking into the app stores for, inter alia, the effectiveness of their measures to prevent minors from accessing age-restricted apps, such as gambling apps.
